Line 264: how worm identity is incorporated into this formula?

body.p: We do not use this formula in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: Line 267: where S_i(t) is the stimulus class i at time window i, i should be t.

body.p: We do not use this formula in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: Line 271-274: throughout the paper, the authors use time (s) and volume interchangeably. This is confusing. Please stick to one metric.

body.p: We no longer use time and volume in the paper. We use units of time.

disp-quote.p: Line 289: linear temporal filter is not defined.

body.p: We provide new filters.

disp-quote.p: Line 349-351: For readers unfamiliar with ref. 41, It is unclear how these different levels of filters are defined and trained.

body.p: We provide new filters and describe how we provide them in the methods section.

disp-quote.p: Line 654: blockstrap should be bootstrap. In addition, how bootstrap methods are implemented to compute the log likelihood ratio is not well described in the methods.

body.p: Thank you for correcting this grammatical error. We no longer implement the method discussed in this original comment; however, we do use bootstrapping in new filters provided in Figure 2 and we discuss how the bootstrapping was done.

disp-quote.p: Line 955 and Line 968: Cannot easily find the graded region and the confidence interval.

body.p: We excluded this from the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Cecere et al. recorded whole-brain activity of immobilized C. elegans exposed to bacterial food stimuli. They performed a few types of analyses to model the neural responses. First, they performed an encoding analysis to model sensory responses to time series of stimuli. Then they performed a decoding analysis to infer stimulus states with a multiclass logistic regression. Finally, to improve upon the linear decoder, they combined the multiclass logistic regression with a soft decision tree to simultaneously decode stimulus state and partition the input into different network states.

The paper addresses an interesting encoding/decoding question with a whole-brain dataset and finds some novel aspects of sensor neuron responses and state dependent motor responses. C. elegans is a nice model organism in which to study these questions, given the recent advances in whole-brain recording and cell identification (e.g. with NeuroPAL). However, I found the technical methods and their presentation lacking. First, it is not clear that the encoding model actually matches and generalizes previous work (38), as claimed. Specifically, the time constant in the proposed model appears to be shared by all states, implying there is effectively one state variable $\Δ(t) = x_1(t) – x_2(t)$, which follows a simple linear ODE. Moreover, there are multiple typos in the equations which make the math hard to follow.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this insightful feedback. In this revised version, we exclude the encoding and decoding models, multi-class logistic regression analysis, and the SDT approach. Instead we use maximum noise entropy to identify stimulus filters and perform dimensionality reduction to identify correlations in activity changes between the various neuronal subtypes and stimuli.

disp-quote.p: The use of the soft decision tree (SDT) is somewhat questionable. The SDT is presented as a method for inferring discrete network states in an unsupervised manner, however, the SDT is a supervised classification method. The authors stack the SDT with a multiclass logistic regression to make a deep decoder, and then use the output after the SDT layer to classify the network states. What I find strange about this is that the SDT already has a multiclass logistic regression as its output layer. Specifically, each leaf node in the SDT outputs a distribution over $K$ discrete labels. I don't see what adding the multiclass logistic regression achieves.

body.p: We agree with the limitation of Soft Decision Trees, especially the redundancy when coupling them with the multi-class logistic regression. We have excluded this analysis from our revised manuscript. Instead we use a BHMDS method which allows us to compare the dimensionality of the network between animals experiencing stimulus and buffer conditions. Additionally, we find that this approach performs better than the more commonly used Principal Component Analysis.

disp-quote.p: I would rewrite the technical methods in the Materials and methods and especially in the main text to be clear, consistent, and accurate. I would also revisit the section on the SDT-MLR hybrid to ensure it is well-motivated and clearly described.

body.p: We have completely revised our manuscript. We no longer use the SDT-MLR approach and opt for Maximum Noise Entropy and Bayesian Hyperbolic Multi-Dimensional Scaling methods instead. The new Methods section for the paper reflects these data analysis we have performed.

disp-quote.p: In addition to the points of confusion described in the public review, there are many details of the encoding model that I find sloppy or unclear. Simply using $[input]$ to describe a potentially time-varying drive is unconventional; it would be more standard to define the input as a function $u(t)$, for example. Sometimes the authors use $*$ and sometimes $\cdot$ to describe scalar multiplication. Finally, I don't see where $g(t)$ is used in the main text or subsequent equations, though I presume it is the output of the proposed model.

body.p: We present an analysis of temporal filters using MNE in the revised manuscript. Additional details along with the relevant equations are included in the Methods section.

disp-quote.p: At the end of the day, the SDT-MLR hybrid seems a bit overkill since the SDT seems to find basically two states of network activity (FWD/REV) with transient states (dorsal/ventral turns?) linking them. Why not just simplify matters and manually cluster the motor activity into these clusters?

body.p: We have eliminated the SDT-MLR hybrid from our analysis, please see the above comments.
[Editors’ note: what follows is the authors’ response to the second round of review.]

disp-quote.p: The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:
Essential Revisions:

1) All recordings were obtained from animals immobilized with tetramisole, and the dynamics of interneurons and motor neurons occur on timescales that are orders of magnitude slower than those observed during natural behavior. Claims that relate neural activity to behavior should therefore be appropriately tempered.

body.p: We acknowledge that the calcium data we obtained was from immobilized animals and that there are differences in magnitude of the neuronal responses compared to animal behavior. Despite this, calcium imaging has been successful in revealing insights into how neural circuits process sensory information to drive behavior. However, as our study did not include behavioral readouts, we have toned down claims relating neural activity to behavior.

disp-quote.p: 2) Methodological refinements. The methodology for identifying representative neurons within each functional cluster should be more clearly quantified and described. In addition, the authors should address other methodological concerns raised by the reviewers.

body.p: We have added additional details in our methods section describing how these representative neurons were identified. First, sensory neurons were identified as those responding when stimulus was presented or removed from the nose of the animals. The two command neurons AVA and RME were easily identified based on their position and expression of different promoters (in the NEUROPAL strain). SMDD and SMDV neurons had fast oscillatory activity patterns that were distinct from other neurons in our recordings and so were placed in a cluster by themselves. In addition, we now include a robustness analysis using unsupervised clustering and show the silhouette scores of both k-means and hierarchical linkage clustering at different values of k, showing that there is no direct best choice of cluster number through fully unsupervised clustering.

disp-quote.p: 3) Clarification of receptive field derivation. The manuscript should explicitly explain how the receptive fields shown in Figure 2 are derived from, and relate to, the parameters of the Maximum Noise Entropy (MNE) model.

body.p: We provide a clarified version of our receptive field derivation 197- 203. We also now provide a schematic representation of the MNE model in revised manuscript Supplementary Figure S2. We also clarify that our plots in Figure 2 represent the first eigenvector of the J matrix parameter of the MNE model and provide this explanation in the results. We focus presentation of the eigenvectors of the J matrix, because they were like h if the linear part was significant, or were much more pronounced than h filters, in cases where neurons were predominantly nonlinear.

disp-quote.p: 4) Comparison between PCA and hyperbolic embedding. A fair and more interpretable comparison between PCA and hyperbolic embedding is needed, including a clearer explanation of what aspects of the data structure each method captures and why hyperbolic space provides additional insight.

body.p: In our revised manuscript, we include a PCA and corresponding Shepard Diagram (comparison plot of distances before and after embedding) along with the hyperbolic embedding from the same animal and for the same number of embedding dimensions. In the new Figure 3, we show the PCA and Shepard Diagram (Figure 3a,b) and hyperbolic embedding (Figure 3,c,d) from the same animal. Figure 3a,b, we show a PCA and Shepard Diagram of a 3-dimensional embedding of a single worm. Notably, the R2 values (compare Figure 3b with 3d) show that hyperbolic embedding can explain more of the variance compared to PCA. In addition, we also include the Shepard diagram for the equivalent 8-dimensional embedding of neural activity in Euclidean (Figure 3e) and hyperbolic space (Figure 3f). Under these conditions with matched dimensionality, hyperbolic continues to provide a better fit than Euclidean embedding. Additionally, we find that the λ of the hyperbolic embedding is 2.38, a value indicative of negative curvature. We find that the negative curvature drives the improvement in fit as opposed to flexibility in the two Shepard diagrams with 8-dimensional embeddings. The curvature parameter of the hyperbolic embedding allows us to fit the data better and the curvature-lacking Euclidean embedding. Therefore, it is not the flexibility of adding extra dimensions that improves quality of fit, but the negative curvature allotted by hyperbolic embedding.

We also compare Bayesian Information Criterion for MDS and HMDS methods, shown below, to test whether adding extra dimensions to Euclidean embedding allows for a better fit to our data. We observe that higher dimensional Euclidean embedding does not achieve a better fit than HMDS without invoking curvature as evidenced by these corresponding BIC plots for both HMDS and Euclidean MDS. We note that the BIC of the Euclidean embedding (left plot) does not improve as one adds dimensions. Collectively we suggest that negative curvature and not flexibility allows hyperbolic embedding to better represent calcium data in C. elegans neurons.

disp-quote.p: 5) Interpretation of hyperbolic geometry and biological relevance. The interpretation of hyperbolic geometry, its relationship to hierarchy, and its relevance to neural circuit organization and biological function should be clarified and more carefully justified.

body.p: We have added clarification in several places in the manuscript that hyperbolic geometry is designed to capture hierarchical aspects of neural population dynamics and make it possible to quantify relative positions within the hierarchy for different interneurons. For example, we find that The interneuron clusters AVA and RME took more central positions in the embedding (Figure 4d) and therefore correspond to more hub like function compared to either sensory on/off neurons or motor-command SMDV and SMDD neurons. Main text changes related to this point are on lines 264-280:

“One of the conceptual advantages of the hyperbolic embedding is that distance from the center of the map can be used to quantify position of a given neuronal cluster in the overall hierarchy of population responses. More specifically, to visualize neural activity in hyperbolic embedding, we used the Poincare ball visualization (Figure 3c). This is a compact representation of a n-dimensional hyperbolic space, in which all the space is mapped into the interior of a unit sphere [42]. We found that neurons belonging to the AVA and RME clusters were close to one another, while those in other clusters were separated. The interneuron clusters AVA and RME had more complex responses and took more central positions in the embedding (Figure 4d). This positioning indicates their hub-like properties within the network [23]. By comparison, motor neurons (SMDD and SMDV) and sensory ON/OFF neurons took more peripheral positions (Figure 4d). We also found that there was a negative relationship between response latency and a cell’s radius in the hyperbolic embedding. The AVA and RME clusters took the longest to respond to bacteria and had smaller radii when compared to ON and OFF sensory clusters. Collectively, these data suggest that the animal movement is likely controlled by the AVA and RME clusters. These neurons in turn might modulate the activity in the SMDD and SMDV neurons. Moreover, activity of AVA/RME interneurons can be biased based on sensory input from ON/OFF neurons allowing for adaptation to distinct states.”

We also include additional details in our revised manuscript (Figure 5) and in the Discussion section. We find that calcium imaging of head neurons in C. elegans provides us with a rich, but high-dimensional dataset. Using Hyperbolic embedding, we can reduce this dimensionality while preserving the original distances between neurons, to a curvature of 2. This curvature is essential to fitting the distances as seen in the Shepard Diagrams (Figure 3d). Curvature in hyperbolic spaces implies that there is a hierarchy in the representational space, the higher the curvature the deeper the hierarchy. We make no claims on the structural organization of the cells; however, we note that previous studies (refs 41,42,43), have reported a hierarchical organization of C. elegans neurons that drive coordinated movements. Moreover, this organization allows for neurons acting at different timescales to interface with each other and drive behavior. Curvature analysis can also reveal principles of neural processing in circuits. For example, if the curvature is increased this can indicate larger number of patterns that can be distinguished based on neural responses. This generates potential prediction for future experiments where animals are exposed and adapted to stimuli ensembles of different variance, with neural responses mapping onto larger hyperbolic maps when produced under stimulation with stimuli with larger variance. We have now included discussion of these points on lines 695-706.

To strengthen the conceptual link between curvature and neural coding we point to Figure 4d in which we see the radii of neural cell types as they are embedded in hyperbolic space. A cell’s radius allows us to determine their position in the hierarchy. For example, cells with smaller radii are higher in the hierarchy and likely play an important role in coordinating information flow. Consistently, we find that AVA and RME neurons have smaller radii compared to sensory neurons indicating that these neurons might play a larger role in coordinating behavior. This hypothesis is consistent with previous studies demonstrating a hierarchical organization in neural circuits driving behavior (refs 41, 42, and 42). Collectively, our analysis provides an unbiased approach to identify the positions of neurons within a hierarchy and their contribution to information processing.

Importantly, we also observed a negative relationship between response latency and radial position (Figure 4d) in the hyperbolic embedding. AVA and RME neurons showed the longest response latencies to bacterial stimuli and were located closer to the center compared to sensory ON/OFF neurons. This organization suggests a functional hierarchy in which sensory neurons provide input to interneuron hubs that coordinate downstream motor outputs. Consistent with this interpretation, AVA and RME activity may modulate the activity of SMDD and SMDV motor neurons, while also integrating sensory input from ON/OFF neurons to enable behavioral adaptation across sensory states.

disp-quote.p: Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):
1. Clarification of receptive field derivation

It is not clear from the text and figures whether receptive fields were computed from the vector h (the linear term), from the dominant eigenvector J (the quadratic term), or from both. Since h and J capture different stimulus-response relationships in the maximum noise entropy (MNE) model, the interpretation of "preferred stimulus features" depends on which term dominates. Please clarify: Which component(s) were used in Figure 2; Whether the "temporally sensitive region" corresponds to h, to an eigenmode of J or a combination; How these choices influence the biological interpretation of sensory vs. motor receptive fields.

body.p: We have clarified now on linear 164-175 and on line 177-178 that Figure 2 shows the leading eigenmode for J. We chose to focus discussion of feature selectivity on the leading eigenvector of J because for these neurons, h filter was either similar to the leading eigenmode of J and non-significantly different from zero. This choice is now clarified on linear 164-175.

disp-quote.p: 2. Fairness and interpretability of the PCA vs. hyperbolic embedding comparison
The comparison in Figure 3 between PCA and hyperbolic embedding would benefit from methodological adjustments:

Metric mismatch: PCA maximizes variance, not distance preservation; Shepard diagrams test pairwise distance reconstruction and are thus not directly suited to PC space. where each neuron is represented by its loadings contributing to the PCs.

body.p: To address this concern, we now include direct comparison between Euclidean and hyperbolic embedding in the same number of dimensions and show their Shepard Diagrams (Figure 3e, f). The Euclidean embedding analyses are carried out in addition to the PCA, which is included here to provide continuity with prior studies [19].
At the same dimensionality (same flexibility) the hyperbolic embedding shows higher R2 than the Euclidean embedding.

disp-quote.p: Dimensionality mismatch: The PCA embedding is 3D, while the hyperbolic embedding is 8D. Dimensionality alone can explain the improved fit.

body.p: We now have performed two comparisons: between PCA and Hyperbolic Embedding in three dimensions and between Euclidean and hyperbolic embeddings in eight dimensions. In both cases, hyperbolic embedding provided a better fit we include these results in Figure 3.

disp-quote.p: Curvature vs. dimensionality: Because of Nash's embedding theorem, hyperbolic spaces can always be embedded in higher-dimensional Euclidean ones. Therefore, a higher-dimensional Euclidean model might achieve similar reconstruction quality without invoking curvature.

body.p: We agree that higher Euclidean model might achieve similar reconstruction quality without invoking curvature. However, we verified that it does not happen for moderately high dimensions, such as eight. In higher dimensions, the dimensionality becomes comparable to the number of neurons, which voids the rationale for dimensionality reduction.

disp-quote.p: Suggested control: Compare Euclidean MDS and Hyperbolic MDS under the same dimensionality (e.g., d=8) and report objective metrics such as stress or R2 in the shepard diagram. The authors could report quantitative measures (e.g., BIC) for Euclidean vs. hyperbolic embeddings under matched conditions.

body.p: Thank you for the suggested experiment, we have performed this and now include these controls in the text on lines 442-448.

disp-quote.p: Additional suggestion: Show how embedding quality varies with curvature parameter λ at fixed dimension to demonstrate that negative curvature, rather than flexibility, drives the improvement.

body.p: We thank you for this suggestion. We have now clarified in the methods section that Bayesian hyperbolic MDS method evaluates a range of curvature values that include zero, and for synthetic Euclidean data, the algorithm has been verified to return essentially zero values <0.001 {Praturu et. al, 2024, iScience}

disp-quote.p: 3. Experimental and interpretational considerations

Behavioral relevance: The animals were immobilized under tetramisole, and interneuron/motor neuron responses occur on much slower timescales than real behavior. Please temper claims about "sensorimotor transformations" or "behavioral outputs" and clarify that the reported structure reflects stimulus-driven network dynamics under immobilization. Line 166-195, any interpretation of the so-called receptive field of AVA and SMD and its connection to foraging behavior is highly speculative.

body.p: To address this concern, we have tempered the correlations between neural activity and behavior and correspondingly edited the text in our revised manuscript. Also, see response to Essential revision 1. Although our data were collected from immobilized animals and might not represent transformations observed in freely moving animals, others and we have found that these calcium imaging experiments reveal insights into information processing and behavioral readouts. However, our current study did not include any behavioral analyses, making it possible to tone down possible implications for behavior.

disp-quote.p: Hierarchical vs. hyperbolic interpretation: While hyperbolic geometry often models hierarchical data, its fit does not by itself demonstrate biological hierarchy. C. elegans neural activity is not obviously hierarchical at the functional level – it's more recurrent. The apparent fit improvement might reflect flexible warping of distances, not a genuine underlying curvature of the neural manifold.

body.p: To address this concern, we added a clarification that hyperbolic geometry also applies to networks with some recurrent interactions [53] i.e. it is not exclusive to feedforward structure. Lines 776-780 in the revised manuscript contain a more in-depth explanation. Nevertheless, the present analyses show that the neural population activity exhibits a globally hierarchical structure and positions AVA and RME in a hub-like role, mediating the connections between sensory and motor-command neurons.

disp-quote.p: Unclustered neurons: The increase in dimensionality under stimulus conditions appears driven by "unclustered" neurons. Please clarify whether these cells contribute meaningful structure or primarily reflect noise.

body.p: We find that the unclustered neurons do contribute to meaningful structure. Specifically, when we remove these neurons in our hyperbolic embedding the dimensionality drops from 8 to 7 dimensions (Figure 4b). These data suggest that the unclustered neurons add on average one additional dimension to the embedding.

disp-quote.p: 4. Methodological refinements

Stimulus autocorrelation: Since the bacterial/buffer sequences differ in temporal statistics, showing the autocorrelation of the stimuli would help interpret the MNE-derived filters and ensure they are not simply recapitulating input correlations.

body.p: To address this concern, we performed a stimulus autocorrelation analysis Below is the plot of the covariance matrix of the stimulus, binned at the appropriate resolution. We note that the matrix shows no significant correlation and appears to be white noise off the diagonal; this is observed due to the randomized setting that orchestrated the onset and duration of the stimulus pulses.

Second, we added a note on line 160-161 that MNE analysis is designed to compensate for stimulus autocorrelation and has been successfully applied with neural responses to natural stimuli that exhibit strong correlations {Rowekamp, Fitzgerald et al. PloS Computational Biology 2011}. The text on line 160-161 now reads: “and which removes stimulus correlations from the estimates of relevant stimulus dimensions computed for each neuron”

disp-quote.p: Cluster robustness: Test cluster stability under different correlation thresholds or with unsupervised clustering (e.g., k-means or hierarchical linkage).

body.p: We used Pearson’s correlation to classify neurons into the various clusters. We agree with the reviewer that there are other approaches to cluster neurons. We used unsupervised clustering to test whether there is a best number of clusters that can be used to classify represent the calcium data.

We analyzed the entire subset of all clustered cells of all 7 worms which experienced stimulus. These “clustered cells” were subjected to k-means clustering analysis, with the calculated silhouette score for each value of “k” in the analysis. We note from the left plot for K-means clustering the lack of an observable “drop” or elbow in inertia, indicating that there is no immediately clear optimal cluster number in which the data should be represented. We also report their silhouette scores on the right plot.
Below we ran a comparative analysis of k-means clustering and hierarchical linkage on the same dataset and report the Silhouette scores of both for every “k”.

We note that although k-means clustering is better representative of the data at any “k”, as denoted by the scores, the scores in general, for both methods and at all reported dimensionalities are low.

disp-quote.p: Dimensionality estimation: Provide uncertainty estimates (e.g., bootstrap confidence intervals) for the "eight-dimensional" embedding to assess robustness.

body.p: We now report the mean and standard deviation for 100 bootstraps of HMDS analysis: 8.02 ± 0.51.

disp-quote.p: 5. Presentation and clarity
Figures 2-3 are dense. Clearer labeling of axes, time units, and which parameters (h or J) are being shown would greatly improve readability.

body.p: We have revised figures 2 and 3 to improve readability. Some of the plots have been moved to supplementary figures. We provide clearer labeling of the axes in Figures 2 and 3. We provide clarification in the text that we are showing the receptive field derived from J matrix of the MNE in each Figure 2 panel.

disp-quote.p: Define key terms such as "sensorimotor transformation" and "hierarchical organization" more precisely to avoid overinterpretation.

body.p: We have removed the term “sensorimotor transformation” from the revised manuscript.

We define hierarchical organization as where activity of one neuron has stronger correlation with another set of neurons than these neurons have with each other. This definition is congruent with the hyperbolic embedding because path of shortest distance between two peripheral points are deflected towards the center of the map where more hub-nodes are located.

Notwithstanding the recurrent interactions, we find that the C. elegans neurons are hierarchically organized, in which the higher-level neurons with slow oscillatory activity modulate lower-level neurons with higher frequency oscillatory activity to perform coordinated movements. These points have now been clarified in the manuscript on lines 268 and 275.

disp-quote.p: Include a schematic overview of the computational workflow to help readers navigate the analytical pipeline. For example, it is unclear what is the purpose from Line 412-429. Is this the only consistent way to average the matrix J across the 4 training sessions?

body.p: We include a schematic overview of the computational pipeline for MNE, Supplementary figure S2 in the revised manuscript.

The subject of lines 412- 429 describes how we obtained 4 separate jackknife estimates and how they were averaged to obtain the single estimate of the stimulus pattern for that neuron. This method is not the only method to average matrix J across 4 training models, but it has been used in prior studies { Kaardal JT, Theunissen FE, Sharpee TO. A Low-Rank Method for Characterizing High-Level Neural Computations. Front Comput Neurosci. 2017 Jul 31;11:68. doi: 10.3389/fncom.2017.00068. PMID: 28824408; PMCID: PMC5534486.} and can be more robust to noise compared to straightforward averaging of the eigenvectors, and it also allows to by pass the issue with undefined sign of the eigenvector.

disp-quote.p: Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

- Because the manuscript proposes a generally applicable analytical workflow, each step should ideally be reproducible and algorithmically defined. The identification of the six representative neuronal classes (ON/OFF, AVA/RME, SMDD/SMDV) forms the foundation for all subsequent analyses. However, compared to the quantitative treatment of receptive fields and hyperbolic embedding, the procedure for selecting representative neurons is described more qualitatively (e.g., 'identified', 'found'). The criteria appear somewhat ad hoc. I recommend explicitly summarizing the decision rules used to define these representative neurons, ideally in a way that is quantitative, algorithmic, and applicable across datasets.

body.p: We have used quantitative metrics to identify the representative neurons in our clusters. Sensory neurons were identified as those that responded to stimulus presentation or removal and SMDD and SMDV neurons had activity patterns that did not cluster with other active neurons in our studies. These two head motor neurons were identified using the NEUROPAL transgenic strain. The AVA and RME clusters had several neurons in each of the animal analyzed. In both clusters, the command neurons AVA and RME were easily identified based on their position and their overlap with the corresponding fluorophores in the NEUROPAL transgenic animal. In addition, we used k-means to designate neurons as either AVA, RME, or unclustered providing an unbiased method for clustering neurons.

disp-quote.p: - The authors show that a hyperbolic embedding provides a better fit to the data than a Euclidean embedding, but the biological meaning of the estimated curvature remains unclear. What does 'strong curvature' correspond to in terms of circuit computation or hierarchical organization? Could curvature change with sensory context in a way that reveals new principles of neural processing? Strengthening the conceptual link between curvature and neural coding would significantly enhance the argument for using hyperbolic geometry.

body.p: Larger curvature in the sensory/motor context corresponds to larger number of discriminable stimuli/motor pattern. We had previous publication that reported increasing curvature with prolonged exposure to an environment.

To strengthen the conceptual link between curvature and neural coding we point to Figure 4d in the revised manuscript, in which we see the radii of neural cell types as they are embedded in hyperbolic space. A cell’s radius allows us to determine their position in the hierarchy. For example, cells with shorter radii are higher in the hierarchy and likely play an important role in coordinating information flow. Consistently, we find that AVA and RME neurons have short radii compared to sensory neurons indicating that these neurons might play a larger role in coordinating behavior. This hypothesis is consistent with previous studies demonstrating a hierarchical organization in neural circuits driving behavior (refs 41, 42, and 42). Collectively, our analysis provides an unbiased approach to identify the positions of neurons within a hierarchy and their contribution to information processing.

disp-quote.p: - Interpretation of hyperbolic coordinates and hierarchy. The manuscript states that interneurons AVA/RME occupy more central positions (smaller radius) whereas ON/OFF sensory neurons, and motor neurons SMDV/SMDD, lie more peripherally (larger radius), and that this reflects differences in latency and hierarchical position. However, the meaning of 'hierarchical' within this embedding is not fully articulated. Does radial distance correspond to circuit depth, integration timescale, or functional influence? Line 57states that 'use a hyperbolic embedding to identify how these clusters interact with each other", but it remains unclear how interactions are inferred from geometry alone. Clarifying how hyperbolic coordinates map onto biological concepts, such as upstream vs. downstream elements, integration timescales, or control hierarchy, would greatly improve interpretability.

body.p: We have clarified in the revised manuscript on lines 375-384 that hyperbolic coordinates correlate with control hierarchy as measured by correlation coefficients. When one node drives two other nodes, the net result on correlation coefficients is that parent node activity is more correlated with the “children” node activities than the children node activities are correlated with each other.
[Editors’ note: what follows is the authors’ response to the third round of review.]

disp-quote.p: The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:
Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I am mostly happy with the revision. There is one important technical point that requires clarification. The distance metric used for hyperbolic embedding d_{ij} = 2(1 – c_{ij}^2) is invariant to the sign of peason correlation coefficient. Neurons that are anti-correlated will be considered functionally as close as those that are positively correlated. This is in sharp contrast with other distance metric such as cosine distance d_{ij} = 1 – c_{ij}. The authors should discuss the biological interpretation of their results within their dataset and why this is a reasonable metric to consider.

body.p: We thank reviewer 1 for bringing attention to this important technical point. The justification for the use of the sign-invariant metric d_{ij} = 2(1 – c_{ij}^2) is twofold. First, this metric generates a proper distance matrix that does not violate triangular inequality. To perform any successful embedding, the distance metric used to compare two points must obey the triangle inequality theorem, which states that the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle must always be greater than the length of the third side. The cosine distance metric d_{ij} = 1 – c_{ij} is known to violate distance inequality. This issue has been studied extensively in bioinformatics for gene embeddings (ref), with the conclusion in favor of the sign-invariant metric that we use. We have verified that the same was true for our dataset: sign-invariant matrix generates essentially zero violations whereas the number of violations increases dramatically for the sign-preserving distance metric (Author response image 5).

The second reason is biological. Although one initially assumes that activity of “opposing” neurons such as On and Off neurons, is anticorrelated, in practice their correlation was closer to zero. The reason is that On neurons are silent when Off neurons are active and vice versa. Because of this approximately “zero” correlation, the neurons are mapped onto opposing parts of the embedding space. The only pair of “opposing” neurons where the embedding results were more nuanced was the AVA/RME pair. The correlation between these neurons was more negative. These neurons embedded into similar regions, but only when data was pooled across animals. When embedding was performed for individual animals, the AVA and RME neurons were separated into opposing parts of the space. These results demonstrate that the sign-invariant metric correctly separates opposing neurons. We have added the discussions of these effects in the manuscript on lines 351-361 and 587-592.

caption.title: Rate of triangle-inequality violations across distance metrics.
caption.p: For each worm in the stimulus condition, we computed pairwise distances between all neurons using five metrics: (1) d = 1 – r (blue), based directly on the raw Pearson correlation coefficient (r); (2) and (3) two lag-sensitive variants (yellow and green) that scan a window of ±50 samples per neuron pair and select either the lag giving the strongest correlation in either direction (sign preserved) or the lag giving the highest positive correlation; (4) a bias-corrected estimate (purple), obtained by applying the Fisher z-transformation to map r onto an unbounded scale where linear extrapolation to infinite data is valid, then transforming back to correlation space and (5) the original metric, 2(1 – r²) (light green), used as a baseline for comparison. Across all worms, the original metric (light green) shows the lowest rate of triangle-inequality violations among the five.
